## 1. Are AI-Built Websites Accessible? What a 15-Site Test Means Before You Launch an AI-Generated Site
- Target keyword: are AI website builders accessible | Secondary: AI generated website accessibility, AI website WCAG check
- Search intent: Commercial investigation
- Format: data-led explainer + pre-launch checklist
- Angle: Small-business owners deciding between an AI builder and a designer hear "it's accessible out of the box." Use the AudioEye test (attributed as a vendor study) and WebAIM's 2026 numbers to show which failures repeat on AI output (keyboard focus, dialogs, form errors, screen-reader labels), give a 30-minute owner check, and say plainly when a designer/dev pass is the cheaper fix. Distinct from the live ADA checklist because it is specifically about AI-generated sites and the DIY-vs-hire decision.
- Why now: AudioEye published on 2026-09-30 that all 15 sites built by five AI tools to a WCAG 2.2 AA brief failed Level A, averaging 55 issues per page — https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/audioeye-study-finds-ai-coding-tools-do-not-write-accessible-code-302893917.html
- Volume / KD: unverified
- Effort: Medium
- Outline starter:
  - H2: What the AI-accessibility test actually found (and who ran it)
  - H2: The five failures that repeat on AI-generated pages
  - H2: A 30-minute accessibility check any owner can run
  - H2: Fix it yourself, prompt it again, or hand it to a designer?
  - H2: What to ask an AI builder or agency before you launch

## 2. Google Now Says Fact-Check All AI Content: A Pre-Launch Review for Website Titles, Meta Descriptions, Alt Text, and Schema
- Target keyword: AI generated alt text review | Secondary: review AI website copy before publishing, AI meta descriptions checklist
- Search intent: Informational
- Format: checklist
- Angle: AI builders now write the invisible parts of a site (titles, meta descriptions, alt text, structured data) that owners rarely read. Turn Google's 2026-10-01 guidance into a field-by-field review sheet for a new or redesigned small-business site, with what to check, common AI mistakes, and who owns each field.
- Why now: Google's Search Central changelog lists "Updated guidance on using generative AI content" on 2026-10-01, and the guide now says it is critical to manually fact-check and review all AI-generated content before publishing — https://developers.google.com/search/updates
- Volume / KD: unverified
- Effort: Low
- Outline starter:
  - H2: What changed in Google's AI content guidance on October 1
  - H2: The site fields AI builders fill in that nobody reads
  - H2: Field-by-field review: titles, descriptions, alt text, schema
  - H2: Red flags that a page was generated and not reviewed
  - H2: Building the review into your launch (DIY vs with a designer)

## 3. How Long Until Google Notices Your Redesign? Realistic Timelines for Titles, Snippets, Canonicals, and Site Moves
- Target keyword: how long does google take to update after website redesign | Secondary: website redesign seo recovery time, how long for google to update title
- Search intent: Informational
- Format: FAQ / timeline explainer
- Angle: Owners panic in the weeks after a relaunch when old titles still show or traffic dips. Explain typical vs slow timelines by change type, framed as figures reported from a Google talk rather than official guarantees, and pair each with what the owner (or their designer) should actually check in Search Console. Complements the live redesign posts by covering the post-launch wait, not the decision or cost.
- Why now: Search Engine Roundtable reported on 2026-10-05 that Gary Illyes showed Google's own timeline data at Search Central Live Deep Dive (for example, title updates typically 1–2 days and site moves 1–3 months typically) — https://www.seroundtable.com/google-crawling-indexing-serving-data-42225.html
- Volume / KD: unverified
- Effort: Medium
- Outline starter:
  - H2: Why your redesign doesn't show up in Google overnight
  - H2: Typical vs slow timelines by change (titles, snippets, canonicals, images, site moves)
  - H2: What slows it down: quality signals and conflicting canonicals
  - H2: A week-by-week post-launch checklist in Search Console
  - H2: When a slow update means something is actually broken

## 4. Service-Area Pages After the September 2026 Spam Update: A Design Worksheet for Location Pages That Aren't Copy-Paste
- Target keyword: service area pages design | Secondary: location pages template duplicate content, small business city pages spam update
- Search intent: Informational
- Format: worksheet / template
- Angle: Page builders make it one click to duplicate a "City + Service" page, which is exactly the pattern that reads as scaled content. Give owners and designers a worksheet for deciding whether a location page deserves to exist and which page sections must be genuinely local (proof, photos, service limits, FAQs), plus when to merge pages instead.
- Why now: Google began the September 2026 spam update on 2026-09-24, with Search Engine Roundtable reporting a second phase on 2026-09-30 — https://www.seroundtable.com/google-september-2026-spam-update-42163.html
- Volume / KD: unverified
- Effort: Medium
- Outline starter:
  - H2: Why duplicated city pages are a risk right now
  - H2: Does this location page deserve to exist? (a 5-question test)
  - H2: The sections that must be genuinely local
  - H2: Merge, rewrite, or noindex: handling the pages you already have
  - H2: Designing a location template that forces real content

## 5. How to Review Your Website Mockups on Your Phone: A Client's Guide to Giving Designers Useful Feedback
- Target keyword: how to give feedback on website design | Secondary: review website mockup on phone, website design feedback checklist for clients
- Search intent: Informational (hire-a-designer stage)
- Format: how-to guide for clients
- Angle: Most small-business clients see their new site design on a phone first and reply with "looks good" or "make it pop." Show how to review mockups on mobile (now easier with Figma's mobile sharing and frame navigation), what to check on each screen, and how to write feedback a designer can act on. Supports `/services/web-design` by showing what working with a designer is like.
- Why now: Figma's 2026-09-30 release added page switching, a frame preview slider, share links to the exact frame, and frame export in its mobile app — https://www.figma.com/release-notes/
- Volume / KD: unverified
- Effort: Low
- Outline starter:
  - H2: Why you should review your site design on a phone first
  - H2: Opening and moving through mockups on mobile
  - H2: A screen-by-screen review checklist (header, CTA, forms, text size)
  - H2: Turning "I don't like it" into feedback a designer can use
  - H2: How many review rounds to expect and what to ask for
